props.title: What makes subscribers stay
props.subtitle: Promise only the ones you deliver. A subscription page that over-promises here is buying churn at full price.

items.title: A predictable rhythm

items.title: An exit without friction

props.title: Subscribe, receive, manage
props.subtitle: Three steps, so the visitor knows what happens after the button and how they stay in control of it.

items.title: Subscribe
items.description: Pick monthly or yearly, pay once, get immediate access to the full back catalogue. The confirmation email states the next charge date.

items.title: Receive
items.description: A new pack on the first Monday, a “new this month” email, and a changelog so you can always see what you paid for.

items.title: Manage
items.description: Switch plans, pause or cancel from the account page. Every change takes effect at the end of the paid period.

items.title: How is this different from a pricing page?
items.description: A pricing page compares plans for someone who already decided to buy. This page has to sell the recurring relationship first: what arrives every month, why it stays valuable, and how easy it is to leave.

items.title: Monthly or yearly first?
items.description: Show both, highlight yearly, and state the saving in plain units — “two months free”, not “17% off”. Let the monthly price anchor the value before the discount lands.

items.title: What happens if I cancel mid-month?
items.description: Access runs to the end of the period you paid for, and the packs you already downloaded stay yours under the same licence. No clawback, no partial refund to chase.

items.title: Trial or money-back window?
items.description: One of the two, never both. A trial suits products people need to use to understand; a refund window suits content. Say it once, near the price, and honour it without friction.

props.title: Get the retention checklist instead
props.subtitle: One email with the six practices above. No sequence, no follow-ups — the plans will still be here.
